_purpose: Scene assembly at a scale a person would not do by hand: three hundred actors placed in one spawn_batch call, counted, and removed again in one delete. The point is not that it is fast - it is that the count the tool reports and the count the world holds are the same number, and that the level is back exactly as it was afterwards. A batch that reports three hundred and leaves two hundred and ninety-eight behind is the failure this is watching for.
_note: Every probe carries a UplinkBulkProbe label, so the counts below are a substring filter over labels rather than a class filter - the marker survives whatever else the level already contains. The deletion at the end names the actors spawn_batch actually returned, via $steps[2].spawned, so it cannot drift from what was made.

steps._why: Clear probes an aborted earlier run may have left. Each entry deletes one matching actor, so the list has to be as long as the batch it is cleaning up after. Deleting nothing is not an error, and a clean project reports zero destroyed.

steps._note: Baseline. If this is not zero the cleanup above did not reach everything, and every count below would be measuring two runs at once.
Three hundred in one request. Kept well below the thousand-actor ceiling so the scenario stays quick, and parked far above the level so nothing lands inside the geometry a template ships with.

The world's own count, read back through a list capped at one row. total_matching keeps counting past the cap and truncated says the list was shortened, so a capped read is never mistaken for the whole set.
Deleted by the names spawn_batch returned, not by the labels this file asked for - so the count can only match if every one of them really was created.
And the level is back where it started.
